title: Persecutions
hookLine: monasteries closed in Tang China and temples torn down in Japan when Buddhism was split from the state

lines: A BRONZE BUDDHA INTO A FURNACE.
cards: A bronze Buddha goes into a furnace and comes out as coins. That scene, or one like it, belongs to a stretch of Chinese history when an emperor of the Tang dynasty turned on the monasteries.

A Japanese monk named Ennin happened to be traveling in China then, and he kept a diary: monks and nuns sent back to lay life, temples emptied, images taken away, foreign monks like himself ordered to leave.
Yesterday the power that protected the sangha also used it. Today it turns against it.

teach.b: Start with China. Under the Tang emperor Wuzong, the court ordered monasteries closed and their lands and metal taken, and monks and nuns were made to return to ordinary life.
Accounts point to more than one reason: money, land, bronze, and court politics that favored other teachings. Ennin's diary is one of the eyewitness sources. Now Japan, much later.

A new government set out to separate Buddhist and Shinto institutions, which had been woven together for a long time, and in some regions a movement rose under a harsh slogan, haibutsu kishaku: abolish the Buddha, destroy Shakyamuni.
Temples were closed or torn down, images burned or sold, and some monks forced out of their robes. Neither story is told to cast anyone as a villain. Each is told because it happened.

teach.h: IT ENDURED, IN HOMES AND CHANTS.
teach.b: Then the second half, today's line: it endured. In China, practice went on, in small temples, in homes, in the chanting of the Buddha's name, and later rulers allowed monasteries again.
In Japan, temples were rebuilt and communities regathered. The Buddha's last words, in the discourse on his final passing, already pointed at this.
In Rhys Davids' translation: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!" Buildings are component things. So is bronze.
So are estates. What came through the furnace was people, still practicing.

how: Buddhist communities in China and Japan remember these persecutions in their histories, and temples that were closed or destroyed have in places been rebuilt and are active today.

games.q: you're a nun in Tang China. the monastery is closed by order, and you're told to return to ordinary life. what keeps the practice alive?
o: nothing: without the monastery it's over.
practice at home, chanting and remembering the teaching.
leaving the teaching behind for good.
games.why: the buildings could be taken; the practice went on in homes and small temples, and later rulers allowed monasteries again.

practice: Bring to mind something in your life, or your family's, that came through a hard time: a recipe carried across a border, a prayer a grandparent kept saying when it wasn't safe, a friendship that survived a bad year.
Notice that the building, the job, the house may be gone, and the thing itself is still here. Breathe with it, and let yourself honor it.

wordCard.voice: Persecutions. Times when rulers turned on monasteries, in Tang China and in Japan, and took the buildings, but not the practice.

orig.note: Japanese haibutsu kishaku: abolish the Buddha, destroy Shakyamuni; the name of the movement against temples.

carryVoice: Your line: it endured. The furnace took the bronze, not the people. See you tomorrow.
